This sounds like a classic thermostat or temperature control issue specific to Hotpoint fridge-freezers (especially older models). The fact that your lettuce and yogurt are frozen solid while presumably other items are okay suggests the cooling is too strong in that zone, or air circulation is blocked.

Here’s a step-by-step troubleshooting guide:

### 1. Check the Thermostat Setting
• Is it set too low? If you have a dial (often numbered 1–5 or 1–7), ensure it’s not on the highest setting ("Max Cold"). Try lowering it by one number and wait 24 hours to see if temperatures stabilize.
• Digital controls: Ensure no "Super Cool" or "Vacation" mode is accidentally activated, which can cause continuous cooling.

### 2. Air Vent Blockage (Most Common Cause)
In most fridge-freezers, cold air from the freezer compartment enters the fridge section through vents at the back.
• Look behind your lettuce and yogurt: Are they pressed directly against the back wall? If so, move them forward.
• Check for ice buildup: Is there a layer of frost or ice on the back panel inside the fridge? This can indicate:
• A defrost problem (see point 3).
• Food items blocking airflow, causing cold air to pool in one spot.

### 3. Defrost System Failure (Very Likely if Ice is Present)
If you see ice/frost on the back wall of the fridge compartment, your defrost system may be failing. Common culprits:
• Defrost heater: Burnt out → won’t melt frost.
• Thermal fuse/cut-out: Tripped or failed → cuts power to the heater.
• Defrost timer/control board: Not initiating the defrost cycle → ice builds up over time, blocking vents and causing uneven cooling (sometimes too cold in spots).

Quick test: Unplug the fridge for 24 hours with doors open to let all ice melt completely. Plug it back in. If the problem returns after a few days/week, you likely have a faulty defrost component (heater, thermostat, or timer).

### 4. Door Seal Issue
• Check if the fridge door seal is tight. A bad seal can cause warm air to enter, leading the compressor to run constantly and overcool in certain areas as it tries to compensate.
• Test: Close the door on a £10 note. If it slips out easily, the seal may be weak.

### 5. Thermostat Sensor Location (If Digital)
Some Hotpoint models have temperature sensors located near the back wall or inside the air ducts. If this sensor is faulty or displaced, it can misread temperatures and overcool specific zones.

---

### What to Do Next:
1. Move food away from the back wall immediately to save your lettuce/yogurt.
2. Lower the thermostat setting slightly if adjustable.
3. Inspect for ice buildup. If you see frost/ice on the back interior panel, this is likely a defrost system failure (heater, fuse, or timer). You’ll need to replace the faulty part.
4. If no ice is visible but it’s still freezing food at the back, try resetting the unit by unplugging it for 10 minutes, then plugging it back in.

### When to Call a Professional:
• If you’re not comfortable opening panels to check/replace defrost heaters or thermal fuses.
• If the fridge is under warranty.
• If the compressor runs constantly without cycling off.

Common Hotpoint Defrost Parts:
Look for "Hotpoint [Your Model Number] defrost heater" or "defrost thermostat." Common part numbers include C5900384 (heater) or C1234567 (thermal fuse), but always verify with your exact model number (found on the rating plate inside the fridge).

That explains everything! If the dial is on Max (usually setting 5 or 7) and food is pressed against the back wall, you have created a "cold trap." The vent is blasting freezing air directly into the produce, which is why your lettuce and yogurt are frozen solid.

Here’s exactly what to do:

### 1. Turn the Dial Down Immediately
• Move the dial from Max down to around 3 or 4 (the middle setting). This is usually the ideal range for most households.
• Wait 2–4 hours before checking if the food has thawed enough to move.

### 2. Rearrange the Food
• Pull everything out of the fridge section slightly.
• Ensure nothing is touching the back wall or blocking the vent slots. Cold air needs space to circulate evenly. If items are packed tight against the vents, they will freeze regardless of the dial setting.

### 3. Check for Hidden Ice (Even if You Didn’t See It)
Since you mentioned there’s no visible ice right now, it might be a thin layer behind the food or on the evaporator plate itself. However, if the problem persists after adjusting the dial and rearranging:
• Unplug the fridge for 24 hours with doors open to ensure any hidden frost melts completely.
• Plug it back in, set the dial to 3–4, and restock without blocking vents.

### Why This Happens
Hotpoint fridges (especially older dial models) often have a strong cooling fan that pulls air from the freezer compartment into the fridge. If the dial is on Max, this airflow is continuous and intense. Combined with food blocking the vent, it creates localized freezing temperatures.

ok did that, turned dial to middle and cleared the vents. after 2 days its better but one yoghurt still froze at the very back. is that normal?

It’s not ideal, but it’s a common leftover issue in Hotpoint fridges with this layout. Here’s why it happens and what to do:

### Why One Yoghurt Still Froze
1. Thermal Lag: The yoghurt likely froze solid before you adjusted the dial. Even after cooling down, frozen items take time to thaw and return to a normal temperature. If it was deeply frozen, it may still feel icy in the center.
2. Airflow Pattern: Cold air from the vent doesn’t distribute perfectly evenly. It often creates a "cold spot" directly behind the first layer of items. If the yoghurt was at the very back, it’s in the primary path of the coldest air.
3. Dial Calibration: The middle setting (e.g., 3 or 4) might still be slightly too cold for your specific fridge model or room temperature.

### What to Do Now
1. Check the Yoghurt: If it’s only partially frozen on one side, that’s normal. Stir it once thawed—it may separate slightly but is usually safe to eat. If it’s rock-hard and icy throughout, it likely froze before you adjusted the dial.
2. Adjust the Dial Further: Try moving the dial down to 2 or even 1 for a day. If temperatures stabilize without freezing anything else, that’s your ideal setting. Hotpoint dials can be sensitive—middle isn’t always "medium" in practice.
3. Create an Air Buffer: Move items with high water content (like yoghurt, milk, or leafy greens) to the middle shelves, away from the back wall. Use the door bins for more resilient items (butter, condiments).

### If It Keeps Happening
If you keep getting frozen spots after adjusting the dial and rearranging:
• Defrost Issue: A failing defrost heater or thermostat can cause uneven cooling. Unplug the fridge for 24 hours to melt any hidden frost behind the back panel.
• Faulty Thermostat: The dial itself might be inaccurate. Use a standalone fridge thermometer to check actual temperatures (ideal is 3–5°C / 37–41°F).
